Ridge: regularized linear regression (cross-validated $\alpha$). This update adjusts routing weights based on current expert performance, but does not reshape h
to favor one expert. Without the A-mediated feedback loop, there is no systematic bias toward

representation space.

D

Adapter Architecture Search (AAS) Details

The AAS loop maintains a population of 20 adapters over 12 generations (∼240 evaluations, 3-epoch
fitness probes). Elitism preserves the top 2; an LLM variant generates candidates in the code space
Gcode . Template-based generation achieves 100% validity (vs. ∼75% for LLM). The 5 canonical
pooling heads used by RR-MoA (mean, last-token, max, attention, Conv1d) were identified as the
most frequent structural motifs across the ∼1,200 candidate adapters explored.

E

485:\textbf{Three architectural instantiations of one principle.} The diagnosis says: restore raw-input access wherever normalization destroyed it. The paper proposes three variants, all confirming the same diagnosis from different angles. \emph{(i)}~\textbf{RR-MoA} (\S\ref{sec:main_results}, Figure~\ref{fig:framework}, headline contribution): external Conv1d gate reads $\mathbf{X}_\mathrm{raw}$ and selects Top-K experts; experts read hidden states $\mathbf{H}$. \emph{(ii)}~\textbf{SR-MoA} (Self-Routed MoA, Figure~\ref{fig:srmoa_arch}, architecture-agnostic validation): no external router, each expert has its own sigmoid gate on $\mathbf{X}_\mathrm{raw}$. \emph{(iii)}~\textbf{Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+}} (Appendix~\ref{app:gate_pathology}, Figure~\ref{fig:residual_ia_arch}, diagnosis-actionability proof): each expert combines a shared NLinear raw-input branch with a gated backbone residual, which closes the DLinear gap.
486-
487-\textbf{The principle is architecture-agnostic (SR-MoA).} To confirm the bottleneck is in the routing \emph{input} rather than the router \emph{architecture}, SR-MoA~\citep{lv2025aoe,cheng2025ermoe,liu2026routingfree} replaces the external Conv1d router with a per-expert sigmoid gate $\sigma_k(\mathbf{X}_\mathrm{raw})$, with no external router at all. SR-MoA \emph{outperforms} RR-MoA by $13$--$42\%$ across all 6 datasets (ETTh1: $0.464$; ETTm1: $0.388$; Weather: $0.222$; 252 runs total), generalizes across six backbones, and independently replicates the Frozen Paradox (frozen best on 4/6 datasets; Table~\ref{tab:self_routed}). That a different architecture exceeds RR-MoA while sharing only the raw-input principle confirms it is the \emph{principle}, not the specific router design, that drives the gains. The same SR-MoA architecture gating on hidden states degrades by $+87\%$ to $+768\%$ on \textbf{all 6 datasets} ($p{=}0.016$, Wilcoxon). \textbf{Normalization-specificity:} on Timer-XL (no RevIN), the same raw-vs-hidden comparison yields only $+4$--$9\%$ ($15$--$100{\times}$ smaller than on MOMENT), confirming the degradation is normalization-induced. A third architecture-level control, \textbf{AdaMix-Raw} (Appendix~\ref{app:adamix_details}), replaces AdaMix's hidden-state router with a raw-input router and recovers entropy to $1.41$--$1.57$ and MSE by $41$--$88\%$ on all 12 cells. All three router instantiations (RR-MoA, SR-MoA, AdaMix-Raw) confirm the same diagnosis: the bottleneck is normalization, not router design. Table~\ref{tab:causal_controls} summarizes all eight converging controls.
488-
--
542:\textbf{Closing the DLinear gap.} DLinear (49K params, from scratch) outperforms frozen adapters in absolute MSE (Table~\ref{tab:baselines}, grey rows). The gap reflects information destruction by the normalization-encoding pipeline (k-NN and Ridge diagnostics in Appendix~\ref{app:diagnostic}), not adapter capacity. As the diagnosis predicts, restoring raw-signal access \emph{at the expert level} closes this gap: \textbf{Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+}} (a dual-stream architecture in which a shared NLinear raw-input branch is added to each expert's output; Appendix~\ref{app:gate_pathology}, Figure~\ref{fig:residual_ia_arch}) matches or beats DLinear on \textbf{6/6 datasets} at $H{=}96$ (up to $-7.5\%$), generalizing to $107/123$ cells across six backbones. A self-routed variant SR-RIA\textsuperscript{+} (Appendix~\ref{app:sr_ria}) achieves the same 6/6 match-or-beat with $3$ outright wins; a TSFM-free Pure Raw-MLP MoE control (Appendix~\ref{app:raw_mlp_moe}) localizes the TSFM's contribution and rules out the alternative hypothesis that the raw branch alone is doing all the work.
543-
544-{\looseness=-1 \textbf{Rawness vs.\ bypass and dose-response.} Replacing the router's raw input with RevIN-normalized input degrades MSE by $60$--$88\%$ while entropy stays high (Table~\ref{tab:router_input}, Appendix~\ref{app:routing_ablations}), confirming the router relies on the \emph{content} of the stripped statistics, not merely the bypass path. A dose-response interpolation $\mathbf{x}_\alpha = (1{-}\alpha)\,\mathbf{x}_\text{raw} + \alpha\,\text{RevIN}(\mathbf{x}_\text{raw})$ reveals a \emph{phase transition} (Figure~\ref{fig:dose_response}; 150 runs): MSE degrades mildly for $\alpha{\leq}0.75$ ($+5.4\%$) but catastrophically at $\alpha{=}1.0$ ($+283\%$), while entropy stays in $[1.43, 1.57]$: normalization renders routing uninformative without reducing diversity. The phase transition threshold is quantitatively predicted at $\alpha^* = R(\mathcal{D})/(R(\mathcal{D})+1) \approx 0.40$ for the median benchmark (Appendix~\ref{app:prop2_depth}). A temporal-shuffle ablation confirms routing depends on $(M,\Sigma)$ statistics, not temporal ordering (Appendix~\ref{app:routing_ablations}).}

362	
363	\subsection{Raw-Routed Mixture of Adapters (RR-MoA)}
364	\label{sec:rrmoa}
365	
366	An \emph{adapter} $g_\phi: \mathbb{R}^{B \times T \times d} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{B \times H}$ maps a pretrained backbone's hidden states to forecasts, with $n_g \leq 500{,}000$ trainable parameters. The goal of per-window routing is to select, for each input window, the subset of expert adapters best suited to that window's characteristics, so that a quiet baseline and a volatile spike are handled by different adapter topologies rather than forced through the same head. As shown in the introduction, this fails when the router reads normalized hidden states, because RevIN removes the per-window statistics that distinguish input regimes. \textbf{RR-MoA} avoids this by splitting the information into two streams: the frozen TSFM produces deep embeddings $\mathbf{H}$ for the experts, while a separate lightweight gate reads the \textit{raw, pre-normalization} input $\mathbf{X}_\text{raw}$ to decide which experts to activate:
367	\begin{equation}
368	\mathbf{Y} = \sum_{j \in \mathcal{T}} \underbrace{\widetilde{w}_j}_{\text{sparse weight}} \cdot \underbrace{\text{Expert}_j(\mathbf{H}_\text{FM})}_{\text{deep embedding branch}},\quad
369	\mathcal{T} = \mathrm{TopK}\!\left(G_\psi(\mathbf{X}_\text{raw}),\, k\right),\;\;
370	\widetilde{w} = \mathrm{softmax}_{\mathcal{T}}\!\left(G_\psi(\mathbf{X}_\text{raw})\right)
371	\label{eq:rrmoa}
372	\end{equation}
373	where $G_\psi$ is a small Conv1d\,+\,pooling\,+\,linear gate ($\sim$1.1K params) operating directly on the raw time series, and each $\text{Expert}_k$ is a canonical adapter head. Routing is restricted to the Top-$k$ experts with the highest gate logits, so only $k$ of $K$ experts execute per sample. With $K{=}5$, $k{=}2$ we obtain $40\%$ of the dense FLOPs while retaining $63\%$ of the dense MSE gain (\S\ref{sec:topk}). The raw input preserves the temporal statistics (trend, amplitude, volatility) that RevIN strips away, enabling per-sample routing that reflects the physical characteristics of each time series window.
374	
375	\textbf{Expert pool.} We maintain $K{=}5$ topologically distinct expert adapters (mean-pool, last-token, max-pool, attention-pool, Conv1d-pool), identified from structural motifs across ${\sim}1{,}200$ architectures in an LLM-guided search (Appendix~\ref{app:aas_details}). Architectural diversity is critical: replacing the five distinct heads with five identical experts (same topology, different initialization) degrades MSE by $8$--$15\%$ (Appendix~\ref{app:diversity}). Pseudocode in Algorithm~\ref{alg:rrmoa} (Appendix~\ref{app:setup}).
376	
377	\section{Experiments}
378	
379	\subsection{Setup}
380	
381	\textbf{Datasets and tasks.} Six LTSF benchmarks (ETTh1/h2/m1/m2~\citep{zhou2021informer}, Weather, Electricity~\citep{godahewa2021monash}) with chronological splits and channel-wise normalization~\citep{nie2023patchtst}. We evaluate forecasting ($H{=}96$) and imputation ($20\%$ masked).
382	
383	\textbf{Backbones.} Five backbones spanning two normalization families: instance-normalized MOMENT-small/large~\citep{goswami2024moment} (internal RevIN~\citep{kim2021revin}); LayerNorm-only Moirai~\citep{woo2024moirai} and Moirai-MoE; and Chronos~\citep{ansari2024chronos} and Timer-XL~\citep{liu2025timerxl} as no-instance-normalization negative controls (\S\ref{sec:cross_backbone}). MOMENT-small is primary. Primary results use a strictly frozen backbone; freeze-level ablations follow.
384	
385	\textbf{Baselines.} Seven baselines: three fixed adapters, LoRA~\citep{hu2022lora} (108-run sweep; Appendix~\ref{app:lora_sweep}), TRACE~\citep{li2025trace}, an independent ensemble of 5 experts, AdaMix~\citep{wang2022adamix} (hidden-state MoE), full fine-tuning (all blocks unfrozen, best of 5 heads $\times$ 2 LRs), and a from-scratch DLinear~\citep{zeng2023dlinear} calibration anchor.
386	
387	\textbf{Training and reproducibility.} Adam, MSE loss, 15 epochs; 5 seeds for the core grid, 3 for ablations. Backbone dimensions, full hyperparameters, and per-baseline configurations: Appendix~\ref{app:setup}. All code, raw JSON results, routing-weight logs, and a self-verification script (\texttt{verify.py}) that re-derives every numerical claim from raw data accompany the submission.
388	
389	\subsection{Main Results}
390	\label{sec:main_results}
391	
392	RR-MoA's case rests on three claims: that fixed-topology adapters are suboptimal, that the natural MoE remedy collapses on instance-normalized backbones, and that the collapse cannot be recovered by standard rescue mechanisms. We establish each in turn before comparing RR-MoA against a comprehensive baseline suite.
393	
394	{\looseness=-1 \textbf{RR-MoA vs.\ fixed adapters.} Table~\ref{tab:rrmoa} compares Top-2 RR-MoA against the best fixed adapter, using the \emph{same five expert heads} in all rows. Across 6 datasets $\times$ 3 freeze levels $\times$ 3 seeds $=$ \textbf{54 configurations}, RR-MoA wins every one with tight standard deviations.}

560	\end{observation}
561	
562	In the limit where the router's signal lives entirely in the stripped statistics ($E \perp\!\!\!\perp S \mid (M,\Sigma)$), the bound saturates and $I(X; E) - I(S; E) = H(E)$: RevIN destroys the entire routing distribution. We therefore use the \emph{signal ratio} $R(\mathcal{D}) = [\mathrm{Var}(M) + \mathrm{Var}(\Sigma)] / \overline{\mathrm{Var}(S)}$ as a tractable monotone proxy for the variance contribution of the stripped statistics. The bound is empirically tight: CCA gives $\varepsilon \in [0.09, 1.26]$ nats, cross-validated within ${\pm}0.26$ nats by KSG~\citep{kraskov2004ksg}; a held-out classifier shows normalization retains only $16$--$41\%$ of routing entropy with bound (ii) gap averaging $0.075$ nats (Appendix~\ref{app:mi_tightness}). Training $\alpha \in [0,1]$ as a learnable parameter, gradient descent converges to $\alpha < 0.5$ on all six datasets ($30/30$ runs; Appendix~\ref{app:learnable_alpha}). $R(\mathcal{D})$ predicts the raw-routing benefit at Spearman $\rho{=}{-}0.88$ ($p{<}0.002$, $n{=}9$; Figure~\ref{fig:signal_ratio}); $H(E \mid S)$ alone does not ($\rho{=}{-}0.12$), since routing \emph{potential} in the stripped statistics matters, not the MI loss itself. Traffic ($R{=}0.14$, $\Delta{=}{+}2.9\%$) is correctly predicted as a boundary case; Solar ($R{=}0.06$) is the one outlier (SSR ablation $+43\%$; Appendix~\ref{app:routing_ablations}). Full proof in Appendix~\ref{app:proofs}.

1	"""Plot the causal contrast figure: MOMENT vs Timer-XL entropy trajectories.
2	
3	4 lines on one panel:
4	  - MOMENT frozen (blue, dashed) — control, entropy stays moderate
5	  - MOMENT last-4 (red, solid) — collapse, entropy → 0
6	  - Timer-XL frozen (green, dashed) — control, entropy stays at max
7	  - Timer-XL last-4 (orange, solid) — NO collapse, entropy stays at max
8	
9	Usage:
10	    python scripts/plot_causal_contrast.py --out figures/causal_contrast.pdf
11	"""
12	
13	import json, math, os, sys
14	import numpy as np
15	import matplotlib
16	matplotlib.use("Agg")
17	import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
18	
19	
20	def load_jsonl(path):
21	    records = []
22	    with open(path) as f:
23	        for line in f:
24	            line = line.strip()
25	            if line:
26	                records.append(json.loads(line))
27	    return records
28	
29	
30	def main():
31	    import argparse
32	    p = argparse.ArgumentParser()
33	    p.add_argument("--moment-frozen", default="results/adamix/trajectory_ETTh1_frozen_42.jsonl")
34	    p.add_argument("--moment-last4", default="results/adamix/trajectory_ETTh1_last4_42.jsonl")
35	    p.add_argument("--timer-frozen", default="results/adamix_timer/trajectory_ETTh1_frozen_42_timer.jsonl")
36	    p.add_argument("--timer-last4", default="results/adamix_timer/trajectory_ETTh1_last4_42_timer.jsonl")
37	    p.add_argument("--out", default="figures/causal_contrast.pdf")
38	    p.add_argument("--K", type=int, default=5)
39	    args = p.parse_args()
40	
41	    log_max = math.log(args.K)
42	
43	    trajectories = {
44	        "MOMENT frozen": (args.moment_frozen, "tab:blue", "--", 1.5),
45	        "MOMENT last-4 (RevIN)": (args.moment_last4, "tab:red", "-", 2.5),
46	        "Timer-XL frozen": (args.timer_frozen, "tab:cyan", "--", 1.5),
47	        "Timer-XL last-4 (no RevIN)": (args.timer_last4, "tab:orange", "-", 2.5),
48	    }
49	
50	    fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 1, figsize=(5.5, 3.5), dpi=150)
51	
52	    for label, (path, color, ls, lw) in trajectories.items():
53	        data = load_jsonl(path)
54	        steps = [r["step"] for r in data]
55	        ent = [r["routing_entropy"] for r in data]
56	        ax.plot(steps, ent, color=color, linestyle=ls, linewidth=lw, label=label)
57	
58	    ax.axhline(log_max, color="gray", linestyle=":", linewidth=0.8,
59	               label=r"$\log K$ (max entropy)")
60	    ax.set_xlabel("Optimizer step", fontsize=11)
61	    ax.set_ylabel("Router entropy (nats)", fontsize=11)
62	    ax.set_ylim(-0.05, log_max + 0.15)
63	    ax.set_xlim(0, 400)
64	    ax.grid(alpha=0.25)
65	    ax.legend(loc="center right", fontsize=8, frameon=True, framealpha=0.9)
66	
67	    # Add annotation for the collapse point
68	    ax.annotate("Collapse\n(step ~40)",
69	                xy=(40, 0.0), xytext=(120, 0.35),
70	                fontsize=8, color="tab:red",
71	                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color="tab:red", lw=1.2))
72	
73	    fig.tight_layout()
74	    os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(args.out) or ".", exist_ok=True)
75	    fig.savefig(args.out, bbox_inches="tight")
76	    print("Saved: %s" % args.out)
77	
78	
79	if __name__ == "__main__":
80	    main()

473	\begin{figure}[h]
474	\centering
475	\includegraphics[width=0.78\columnwidth]{figures/causal_contrast.pdf}
476	\vspace{-4pt}
477	\caption{\textbf{Causal contrast: MOMENT vs Timer-XL} (ETTh1, last-4 unfreezing). MOMENT entropy collapses $0.51{\to}0.000$ in ${\sim}40$ steps (red); Timer-XL stays at ${\approx}1.60$ for all $400$ steps (orange). Same code, same data, only normalization differs. Pattern generalizes across all 3 tested datasets.}
478	\label{fig:causal_contrast}
479	\end{figure}
480	
481	In contrast, \textbf{RR-MoA} maintains healthy routing entropy ($1.0$--$1.57$) and wins \textbf{54/54} configurations, with MSE improvements of $27\%$ to $77\%$ over the best fixed adapter. Notably, on Traffic ($R{=}0.14$, where the stripped statistics carry little information), RR-MoA does not improve over fixed adapters, exactly as Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp} predicts (Figure~\ref{fig:signal_ratio}).
482	
483	\textbf{Rescue-baseline sweep.} To rule out that the collapse is merely under-tuned, we sweep five standard MoE rescue families (Switch load-balance~\citep{fedus2022switch}, ST-MoE z-loss~\citep{zoph2022stmoe}, entropy regularization, ReMoE ReLU routing~\citep{zhang2025remoe}, and expert-choice routing~\citep{zhou2022expertchoice}) across eleven configurations on 6 datasets $\times$ 2 freeze levels $\times$ 5 seeds $= 720$ runs (Table~\ref{tab:rescue}, Appendix~\ref{app:rescue_details}). The best rescue (z-loss $c_z{=}0.01$) reduces MSE by only $10.9\%$, still $2.7{\times}$ worse than RR-MoA. Excessive balancing ($\alpha{=}10.0$) is catastrophic ($+67.7\%$). This confirms Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}(ii): when routing information is structurally absent from the hidden states, none of the standard rescue mechanisms we tested can compensate.
484

# Visual-Error Audit: `main.pdf` (44 pages, 10 figure-pages inspected)

Workflow: rendered PDF → 200 DPI per-page PNGs in `/tmp/paper_review_screenshots/` → 4 parallel subagents inspected pages {2, 4} / {6, 7} / {9} / {17, 20, 21, 27} → I verified the high-priority findings against TikZ/Python source and rendered images.

---

## Confirmed major issues (3) — fix before submission

### M1. Fig 2 (p4): Path A arrows contradict the caption
- **Source**: `main.tex:333,335,337` use `\draw[grayarr]` for H→{E1,E3,E5}; lines 334,336 use `\draw[bluearr]` for H→{E2,E4}.
- **Caption** (line 357): "*Path A (blue): frozen TSFM produces H for **all experts***" — but only the active experts get blue rails; inactive ones get gray, which a reviewer reads as "H is not delivered to E1/E3/E5".
- **Fix**: change `grayarr` → `bluearr` on lines 333, 335, 337. The activation status is already conveyed by the dashed expert box style; gray rails are over-encoding.

### M2. Fig 4 (p7): caption describes 2 curves, plot shows 5
- **Source**: `scripts/plot_causal_contrast.py:43-47` plots 4 curves (MOMENT frozen, MOMENT last-4 RevIN, Timer-XL frozen, Timer-XL last-4 no-RevIN) plus a `log K` reference line at 1.609 (line 58-59).
- **Caption** (`main.tex:477`) only mentions the red MOMENT and orange Timer-XL curves; the two dashed frozen controls and the `log K` line are unexplained.
- **Fix**: amend the caption to one sentence acknowledging the controls — e.g., "*Dashed: frozen controls for both backbones (no collapse). Dotted: log K = 1.609 ceiling.*" — OR regenerate the PDF with only the two unfrozen curves.

### M3. Fig 5 (p9, right): boundary cases not visually marked
- **Source**: `main.tex:613-616` plots all 9 points with the same `mark=*, blue!80` style. Caption explicitly calls out *Traffic and Solar* as boundary cases; only their text labels distinguish them.
- **Fix**: at line 614, split the `coordinates {…}` block so Traffic and Solar use a different mark (e.g., `mark=square*, mark size=3pt, red!70!black`); then the caption claim is visually grounded. Optionally annotate Solar with "(outlier)" to match prose at line 562 ("the one outlier").

---

## Confirmed minor issues (12) — polish

| # | Page / Fig | Element | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| m1 | p9 / Fig 5 right | "m1" (`main.tex:620`) and "W" (`main.tex:621`) labels both at x≈0.70, overlapping | Move "W" to `anchor=east` and shift x by −0.02, or stack vertically. |
| m2 | p9 / Fig 5 left | Legend `at={(0.02,0.98)}` (line 580) sits over the −36 % ETTh1 label (line 589) | Move legend to `anchor=north east, at={(0.98,0.98)}`. |

| m5 | p6 / Fig 3 | Internal panel titles "(a) Router entropy trajectory" / "(b) Per-expert gradient norm" duplicate the LaTeX caption | Remove `ax.set_title(...)` calls in `scripts/plot_adamix_trajectory.py` and regenerate. |
| m6 | p6 / Fig 3b | Legend overlaps upper curves | Move legend to `loc='lower right'` in plot script. |
| m7 | p17 / dose response (Fig E.1) | No ±std bands despite "5 seeds" claim | Either add shaded `\addplot+[name path=…]` confidence bands at lines 1130-1135, or add caption clause "(std smaller than marker)". |

## Cross-figure consistency

- **FROZEN badge convention**: page 20 (SR-MoA) puts it at `tsfm.north west`, page 27 (Residual-IA+) at `tsfm.north east` with explicit shift (line 2161). Pick one — recommend `north east` everywhere — and apply to both files plus Fig 2 (line 281, RR-MoA) for a uniform vocabulary across the three architecture diagrams.
- **Active/inactive convention**: Fig 2, SR-MoA, and Residual-IA+ each use a slightly different mix of (i) arrow color, (ii) arrow dashing, (iii) box dashing to flag inactive experts. Standardize on **box dashing only** to encode active/inactive; arrows stay uniform within each stream.

1	"""T2.A visualization: plot per-step routing / gradient trajectories
2	produced by ``run_adamix.py --trajectory ...``.
3	
4	Reads two JSONL files (an "unfrozen" collapse case and a "frozen" control)
5	and produces a single two-panel figure:
6	
7	    Panel (a): routing entropy over optimizer steps, one line per setting.
8	    Panel (b): per-expert gradient L2 norm over steps, collapse case only
9	               (to show that one expert's gradient dominates and the others
10	               rapidly starve). A dashed line gives the sum of the other 4
11	               experts for reference.
12	
13	Usage::
14	
15	    python scripts/plot_adamix_trajectory.py \
16	        --collapse results/adamix/trajectory_ETTh1_last4_42.jsonl \
17	        --control  results/adamix/trajectory_ETTh1_frozen_42.jsonl \
18	        --out figures/adamix_trajectory.pdf
19	
20	The output PDF is intended to be dropped into ``main.tex`` as a standalone
21	figure between Tables 4 and 5, upgrading the gradient co-adaptation claim
22	from correlational (Table 4 entropies at epoch end) to mechanistic.
23	"""
24	
25	import argparse
26	import json
27	import math
28	import os
29	import sys
30	
31	import numpy as np
32	import matplotlib
33	matplotlib.use("Agg")
34	import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
35	
36	
37	def load_jsonl(path):
38	    records = []
39	    with open(path) as f:
40	        for line in f:
41	            line = line.strip()
42	            if not line:
43	                continue
44	            records.append(json.loads(line))
45	    return records
46	
47	
48	def plot_trajectory(collapse_path, control_path, out_path, K=5):
49	    collapse = load_jsonl(collapse_path)
50	    control = load_jsonl(control_path) if control_path else None
51	
52	    max_steps = max(len(collapse), len(control) if control else 0)
53	    log_max = math.log(K)
54	
55	    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.5, 3.3), dpi=150)
56	
57	    # --- Panel (a): routing entropy over steps ---
58	    ax = axes[0]
59	    steps_c = [r["step"] for r in collapse]
60	    ent_c = [r["routing_entropy"] for r in collapse]
61	    ax.plot(steps_c, ent_c, color="tab:red", linewidth=2,
62	            label="AdaMix, last-4 unfrozen (ETTh1)")
63	    if control is not None:
64	        steps_f = [r["step"] for r in control]
65	        ent_f = [r["routing_entropy"] for r in control]
66	        ax.plot(steps_f, ent_f, color="tab:blue", linewidth=2,
67	                label="AdaMix, strictly frozen (ETTh1, control)")
68	    ax.axhline(log_max, color="gray", linestyle=":", linewidth=1,
69	               label=r"$\log K = \log 5$ (uniform max)")
70	    ax.set_xlabel("Optimizer step")
71	    ax.set_ylabel("Router entropy (nats)")
72	    ax.set_title("(a) Router entropy trajectory")
73	    ax.set_ylim(-0.05, log_max + 0.1)
74	    ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
75	    ax.legend(loc="best", fontsize=7, frameon=True)
76	
77	    # --- Panel (b): per-expert grad norm for the collapse case ---
78	    ax = axes[1]
79	    grad_matrix = np.array([r["expert_grad_norms"] for r in collapse])  # (T, K)
80	    colors = ["tab:red", "tab:orange", "tab:green", "tab:blue", "tab:purple"]
81	    labels = ["Mean", "Last", "Max", "Attn", "Conv1d"]
82	    # Order by peak gradient norm -> the dominant expert becomes the red line
83	    peak_idx = np.argsort(-grad_matrix.max(axis=0))
84	    for rank, k in enumerate(peak_idx):
85	        style = "-" if rank == 0 else "--"
86	        lw = 2.0 if rank == 0 else 1.0
87	        alpha = 1.0 if rank == 0 else 0.7
88	        ax.plot(steps_c, grad_matrix[:, k], color=colors[rank % len(colors)],
89	                linestyle=style, linewidth=lw, alpha=alpha,
90	                label=("%s (dominant)" % labels[k]) if rank == 0 else labels[k])
91	    ax.set_xlabel("Optimizer step")
92	    ax.set_ylabel(r"$\|\nabla_{\phi_k}\mathcal{L}\|_2$")
93	    ax.set_title("(b) Per-expert gradient norm (last-4 unfrozen)")
94	    ax.set_yscale("log")
95	    ax.grid(alpha=0.3, which="both")
96	    ax.legend(loc="best", fontsize=7, frameon=True, ncol=2)
97	
98	    fig.tight_layout()
99	    os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(out_path) or ".", exist_ok=True)
100	    fig.savefig(out_path, bbox_inches="tight")
101	    pdf_path = out_path
102	    if not out_path.endswith(".pdf"):
103	        pdf_path = os.path.splitext(out_path)[0] + ".pdf"
104	        fig.savefig(pdf_path, bbox_inches="tight")
105	    print("Saved: %s" % out_path)
106	    return out_path
107	
108	
109	def main():
110	    p = argparse.ArgumentParser()
111	    p.add_argument("--collapse", required=True,
112	                   help="JSONL trajectory for an unfrozen / collapse condition")
113	    p.add_argument("--control", default=None,
114	                   help="JSONL trajectory for the frozen / control condition")
115	    p.add_argument("--out", default="figures/adamix_trajectory.pdf")
116	    p.add_argument("--K", type=int, default=5)
117	    args = p.parse_args()
118	
119	    plot_trajectory(args.collapse, args.control, args.out, K=args.K)
120	
121	
122	if __name__ == "__main__":
123	    main()
124	
```

1116	For $\alpha < \alpha^*$, routing quality degrades continuously; for $\alpha \to 1$, routing collapses discontinuously due to the softmax's exponential sensitivity to signal-to-noise ratio.
1117	\end{proposition}
1118	
1119	\emph{Validation.} For the median $R(\mathcal{D}) = 0.67$ across our benchmarks, Proposition~\ref{prop:phase_transition} predicts $\alpha^* \approx 0.40$. The dose-response experiment (Figure~\ref{fig:dose_response}; 150 runs) confirms this: MSE degrades mildly for $\alpha \leq 0.75$ ($+5.4\%$) but catastrophically at $\alpha = 1.0$ ($+283\%$). The sharpness of the transition arises from the softmax: when $P_\mathrm{route}(\alpha) / P_\mathrm{noise}$ drops below ${\sim}1$, routing weights converge to uniform regardless of expert relevance.

1455	\textbf{What the router learns.} Per-sample routing decisions correlate with amplitude and volatility, the very statistics RevIN strips (Figure~\ref{fig:routing_viz}). On ETTh1, Expert~0 (mean-pool) serves as the generalist ($53\%$), while Expert~2 (max-pool) handles low-amplitude windows and Expert~3 (attention-pool) handles high-amplitude windows. The router reserves specialized processing for windows at the distribution tails, empirically validating the conditional independence assumption $E \perp\!\!\!\perp S \mid (M,\Sigma)$ of Part~(iii) of Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}.

Expert selection clusters by amplitude and volatility (the very statistics RevIN strips), empirically validating the conditional independence assumption $(M,\Sigma) \perp\!\!\!\perp S$ from Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}(iii).}

2250	\caption{\textbf{Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+} architecture (dual-stream extension).} \textit{Stream 1} (blue): the frozen TSFM produces hidden states $\mathbf{H}$, fed into each expert's Adapter head. \textit{Stream 2} (green): a shared NLinear branch reads $\mathbf{X}_\mathrm{raw}$ directly, producing $\mathbf{y}_\mathrm{raw}$ — DLinear-equivalent and shared across all $K$ experts. Each expert combines them as $\mathbf{y}_k = \mathbf{y}_\mathrm{raw} + \sigma(\mathrm{blend}_k(\mathbf{X}_\mathrm{raw})) \cdot \mathrm{Adapter}_k(\mathbf{H})$, with the blend gate initialized at $b{=}{-}2$ so the model starts as effectively-DLinear and learns to add backbone signal where useful. Self-routing $\sigma$ gates (orange) on $\mathbf{X}_\mathrm{raw}$ select which experts contribute. Result: \textbf{6/6 vs DLinear at $H{=}96$} on MOMENT-small; \textbf{107/123 cells} ($88\%$) match-or-beat across 6 backbones $\times$ 6 datasets $\times$ 4 horizons (Tables~\ref{tab:residual_ia_plus}, \ref{tab:residual_ia_plus_mhcb}).}
2251	\label{fig:residual_ia_arch}
